paragraphs: In May 1967 Pakistan harvested 600,000 acres to new high-yielding wheat seed. … In 1967 the new high-yielding wheats were harvested from 700,000 acres in India. This year they will be planted to 6 million acres. … India will harvest more than 95 million tons in food grains this year—again a record crop. …

These and other developments in the field of agriculture contain the makings of a new revolution. It is not a [violent] Red Revolution like that of the Soviets, nor is it a White Revolution like that of the Shah of Iran. I call it the Green Revolution.

This new revolution can be as significant and as beneficial to mankind as the industrial revolution of a century and a half ago. … Good luck—good monsoons—helped bring in the recent record harvests. But hard work, good management, and sound agricultural policies in the developing countries and foreign aid were also very much involved. …

[A new rice variety called] IR-8 has a stiff, strong, short straw. It does not fall over, or lodge, when the plant is heavily fertilized or when it is buffeted by wind and rain. It matures quickly, allowing for two—sometimes three—crops in a single year. …

But the developing nations—their governments, their institutions, and their farmers—cannot sustain the Green Revolution without outside support. They lack the skills to do the necessary adaptive research. They lack the capital to build fertilizer plants. They lack the facilities and the technicians needed to train their people in the new ways. …

To the farmer, the new seeds and fertilizer represent an untried and expensive investment. The high yields of IR-8 depend on a combination of intensive labor and materials which makes it four times as costly to [grow] as ordinary rice. Only when the farmer sees that the added investment will increase his profit will he give them a try. …

paragraphs: There is ample evidence during the first epidemic of the introduction of infection into a locality from another infected locality. The railway played a prominent part as was inevitable. During the panic caused by the epidemic the trains were filled with emigrants from infected centres, many of them being ill. The Post office also was an important agency in disseminating infection, also very largely through the Railway Postal Service. … Marwari traders, shopkeepers and even doctors, in fact all who travelled by water, road or rail, were potential factors in distributing infection.

There is no method by which the deaths actually due to influenza can be calculated. If it be assumed that the excess in the deaths in 1918 over the mean of the previous 5 years was the result—direct or indirect—of influenza, the figure would come to 7,718,307. This is an overestimate owing to the disturbing factor of other epidemic diseases, such as plague, cholera, malaria and relapsing fever … . Without any claim to accuracy it is suggested that the mortality directly and indirectly due to influenza was in the neighbourhood of … 7,089,694.*

When it is remembered that the epidemic struck India suddenly and almost universally it will be realised to what extent the medical organization already thinned by military needs was taxed. … The failure to meet the demand [for doctors] was due to two causes: (a) the necessity for supplying medical officers for the war. A similar need depleted the civil medical practitioners in all countries taking part in the late struggle, (b) the Medical Colleges and Schools in India cannot turn out a sufficient number of medical men to meet the normal demand. …
Rural areas depend for their medical aid on dispensaries, and these dispensaries are, speaking for India as a whole, too widely separated to be of general utility in a wide spread epidemic.

paragraphs: … The spread of information networks is forming a new nervous system for our planet. When something happens in Haiti or Hunan, the rest of us learn about it in real time—from real people. And we can respond in real time as well. …

Now, in many respects, information has never been so free. There are more ways to spread more ideas to more people than at any moment in history. And even in authoritarian countries, information networks are helping people discover new facts and making governments more accountable. …

… In the last year, we've seen a spike in threats to the free flow of information. China, Tunisia, and Uzbekistan have stepped up their censorship of the internet. In Vietnam, access to popular social networking sites has suddenly disappeared. …

P2.title: Total Fertility Rate in Selected Countries, 1970 and 2023 (average births per woman)
P2.text: The total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime if she had children at the rates of that year. Where few children die, a rate of about 2.1 births per woman replaces one generation with the next; a population can still grow or shrink for years because of its age mix and migration. These World Bank figures draw on United Nations estimates and other official population statistics. The world average was 4.8 in 1970 and 2.2 in 2023.
P2.source: World Bank, World Development Indicators, "Fertility rate, total (births per woman)" (indicator SP.DYN.TFRT.IN), from United Nations, World Population Prospects, and national statistical offices; data updated October 2026; CC BY 4.0

paragraphs: … There is little doubt that the present Chinese leadership led by Deng Xiaoping is most determined to push forward with a rapid pace of modernization. They consider close trade and economic relations with the United States as essential for this purpose. …

… Few would have imagined that the exploitation of the world's abundant resources and a prodigious growth in world trade would have seen the gap between rich and poor widening. And few could have anticipated the burden of debt on many poor nations.

Whereas disregard and contempt for human rights have resulted in barbarous acts which have outraged the conscience of mankind, and the advent of a world in which human beings shall enjoy freedom of speech and belief and freedom from fear and want has been proclaimed as the highest aspiration of the common people, …
Now, therefore, The General Assembly, Proclaims this Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations … .
Article 1. All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. …

Article 2. Everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in this Declaration, without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status. …

Article 21. … The will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government; this will shall be expressed in periodic and genuine elections which shall be by universal and equal suffrage … .
Article 26. Everyone has the right to education. Education shall be free, at least in the elementary and fundamental stages. …

paragraphs: The closing paragraphs of this book were written in the late summer of 1914, when the armies of every great power in Europe were being mobilised for savage, unsparing, barbarous warfare … . How mild, by comparison with the despatches in the daily newspapers, will seem this chronicle of women's militant struggle against political and social injustice in one small corner of Europe. …

… The militancy of men, through all the centuries, has drenched the world with blood, and for these deeds of horror and destruction men have been rewarded with monuments, with great songs and epics. The militancy of women has harmed no human life save the lives of those who fought the battle of righteousness. …

This we know, that in the black hour that has just struck in Europe, the men are turning to their women and calling on them to take up the work of keeping civilisation alive. Through all the harvest fields, in orchards and vineyards, women are garnering food for the men who fight, as well as for the children left fatherless by war. In the cities the women are keeping open the shops, they are driving trucks and trams, and are altogether attending to a multitude of business.
When the remnants of the armies return, when the commerce of Europe is resumed by men, will they forget the part the women so nobly played? …

… the struggle for the full enfranchisement of women has not been abandoned; it has simply, for the moment, been placed in abeyance. When the clash of arms ceases, when normal, peaceful, rational society resumes its functions, the demand will again be made. If it is not quickly granted, then once more the women will take up the arms they to-day generously lay down. There can be no real peace in the world until woman, the mother half of the human family, is given liberty in the councils of the world.
P14.attribution: Emmeline Pankhurst, founder of the Women's Social and Political Union, a British women's organization, foreword to her memoir, My Own Story, published in London and New York in 1914

paragraphs: … It is based on a realisation that the cinema is to-day the most universal means through which national ideas and national atmosphere can be spread, and, even if those be intangible things, surely they are among the most important influences in civilisation. … To-day films are shown to millions of people throughout the Empire and must unconsciously influence the ideas and outlook of British peoples of all races. But only a fraction, something like 5 per cent., of the films which are at present shown in the British Empire are of British origin. That, as I submit and as the Imperial Conference held, is a position which is intolerable if we can do anything effective to remedy it.

From the trade point of view, the influence of the cinema is no less important. It is the greatest advertising power in the world. Just let the House imagine the effect upon trade of millions of people in every country, day after day, seeing the fashions, the styles, and the products of a particular country. It inevitably influences them in their trade purchases. …

… Our Trade Commissioner in New Zealand, in his most recent report, writes: "Even in New Zealand, with its staunch British traditions, one finds evidences that customs and the demand for goods are being largely influenced by changes in ideas and fashions other than those associated with British habits and tastes. … there seems little doubt that American films have played a part in moulding public tastes in many directions." …

If that be at all true of the importance of this matter from a trade point of view, I submit that the need for the development of the British film, from a national point of view and from a trade point of view, is firmly established; and if it cannot be developed without Government intervention, then, I submit, the case for Government intervention is made out.

paragraphs: 5. We believe that the central challenge we face today is to ensure that globalization becomes a positive force for all the world's people. For while globalization offers great opportunities, at present its benefits are very unevenly shared, while its costs are unevenly distributed. We recognize that developing countries and countries with economies in transition face special difficulties in responding to this central challenge. … These efforts must include policies and measures, at the global level, which correspond to the needs of developing countries and economies in transition and are formulated and implemented with their effective participation.

6. … Shared responsibility. Responsibility for managing worldwide economic and social development, as well as threats to international peace and security, must be shared among the nations of the world and should be exercised multilaterally. As the most universal and most representative organization in the world, the United Nations must play the central role. …

To ensure that, by the same date, children everywhere, boys and girls alike, will be able to complete a full course of primary schooling … . practice.stem: Eisenhower's proposal was made most directly in response to

options.A: the end of the Korean War, which left Korea divided between communist and noncommunist governments
options.B: a shortage of coal and oil that slowed Western Europe's recovery after the Second World War
options.C: the spread of nuclear power plants to many newly independent countries in Asia and Africa
options.D: a growing nuclear arms race after the Soviet Union tested its own atomic bombs

practice.explanation: The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in 1949. Both superpowers then built hydrogen bombs, which were far more powerful. Eisenhower hoped to turn some of this dangerous knowledge to peaceful uses and to show that the United States wanted peace.

whyNot.A: The Korean War ended in July 1953, but Eisenhower's speech is about atomic weapons, not Korea.
whyNot.B: Europe did need more energy, but Eisenhower is speaking to the whole world about the "fearful trend of atomic military buildup."
whyNot.C: In 1953 no country in Asia or Africa had a nuclear power plant. Eisenhower hoped to bring power to these "power-starved areas" in the future.

practice.hint: Reread the first sentence. What trend worried Eisenhower, and what had caused it?

practice.stem: The proposal in the third paragraph most directly reflects which broader development after 1945?

options.A: The division of Europe into rival military alliances led by the United States and the Soviet Union
options.B: The creation of international organizations to deal with problems that crossed national borders
options.C: The spread of import substitution policies in newly independent countries
options.D: The independence of India, Pakistan, and other colonies in South Asia after the Second World War

practice.explanation: Eisenhower asked for a new agency "under the aegis of the United Nations" to share nuclear materials for peaceful uses. The International Atomic Energy Agency was founded in 1957. It was one of many international groups formed after 1945, along with the UN, the World Bank, and the World Health Organization, to handle problems no single country could solve.

whyNot.A: NATO and the Warsaw Pact were military alliances on opposite sides. Eisenhower wants an agency that includes both the United States and the Soviet Union.
whyNot.C: Import substitution (making goods at home instead of buying them from other countries) was an economic policy of single countries. It was not an international agency.
whyNot.D: Independence in South Asia was part of decolonization. Eisenhower's proposal is about sharing atomic materials through the UN.

practice.hint: Decide what kind of body Eisenhower is proposing. Is it an alliance, one country's policy, or something else?

practice.stem: Which of the following later developments would most directly challenge Eisenhower's hope that atomic energy would "serve the needs rather than the fears of mankind"?

options.A: France came to produce most of its electricity in nuclear power plants built after the oil crises.
options.B: Doctors expanded the use of radioactive materials to find and treat cancer.
options.C: The 1986 accident at the Chernobyl nuclear plant spread radiation over large areas.
options.D: Inspectors from an international agency checked nuclear plants for signs of secret weapons work.

practice.explanation: The Chernobyl disaster in the Soviet Union forced more than 100,000 people from their homes and spread radiation across Europe. Accidents like it, and the one at Fukushima in Japan in 2011, made many people fear nuclear power.

whyNot.A: Electricity from nuclear plants is the kind of peaceful use Eisenhower hoped for. This supports his hope.
whyNot.B: Eisenhower names "medicine" as a peaceful use. This supports his hope.
whyNot.D: Inspections helped keep nuclear power peaceful. This supports his hope.

practice.hint: Reread the last sentence of the fourth paragraph. What kind of event would show the opposite of what Eisenhower hoped for?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a pattern shown in the chart?

options.A: Fertility rates fell the most in the countries that were already wealthy in 1970.
options.B: Fertility rates in the Asian countries shown stayed higher than in the African country shown.
options.C: Fertility rates rose in countries with large farm populations, such as India and Bangladesh.
options.D: Fertility rates fell in every country shown, most to about two children per woman or fewer.

practice.explanation: In 1970 most of these countries had fertility rates of five or more births per woman. By 2023, eight of the nine had rates of 2.2 or lower. This was one of the biggest social changes of the period.

whyNot.A: The United States fell by less than one child per woman. Iran, Mexico, and China fell by more than four.
whyNot.B: Nigeria, in Africa, had the highest rate in 2023 (4.5). Each Asian country shown was lower.
whyNot.C: India fell from 5.6 to 2.0, and Bangladesh from 6.8 to 2.2.

practice.hint: Compare the two bars for each country. Did they go up or down, and by how much?

practice.stem: Which of the following most directly contributed to the changes shown for most countries?

options.A: The Green Revolution, which let farm families grow enough food to feed more children
options.B: A rise in deaths of young children from new diseases such as HIV/AIDS
options.C: China's one-child policy, which limited most urban families to a single child
options.D: Wider use of modern birth control and more schooling for girls

practice.explanation: New birth control pills and devices spread after the 1960s and gave women more control over having children. More girls went to school, and more women worked outside the home. As fewer babies died, parents also chose to have fewer children.

whyNot.A: The Green Revolution did grow more food. But more food would make it easier to raise big families, not lead to smaller ones.
whyNot.B: Deaths of young children fell in most countries. When fewer children die, parents tend to have fewer children.
whyNot.C: China did limit births by law starting in 1980. But Iran, Brazil, Mexico, and Bangladesh lowered their rates without such a law.

practice.hint: The question asks about most of the countries, not just one. Which choice could explain a change that happened in so many places?

practice.stem: The data in the chart would best support which of the following arguments about the period after 1970?

options.A: Fertility fell in countries with different religions, governments, and levels of wealth.
options.B: Religious traditions kept fertility rates high in the countries shown where most people are Muslim.
options.C: Fertility rates fell mainly in the countries that were ruled by communist parties at the time.
options.D: Fertility rates fell faster in Africa than in Asia or Latin America.

practice.explanation: Falling fertility rates spread across Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East. Iran's rate fell from 6.8 to 1.7, helped by a government family planning program restarted in 1989. Fertility fell in many very different societies.

whyNot.B: Iran and Bangladesh, where most people are Muslim, had some of the biggest drops.
whyNot.C: Brazil, Mexico, Iran, and South Korea were not communist, yet their rates fell sharply.
whyNot.D: Nigeria, the only African country shown, fell by 2.0 births per woman, less than any Asian or Latin American country shown. One country also cannot show a pattern for a whole continent.

practice.hint: Look at where the countries with the biggest drops are, and what kinds of governments and religions they have.

practice.stem: The scene in the photograph is best understood in the context of

options.A: the U.S. Army's campaigns against yellow fever during the building of the Panama Canal
options.B: the U.S. Army's expedition into Mexico in 1916 to chase the rebel leader Pancho Villa
options.C: the First World War, when crowded army camps and troopships spread disease around the world
options.D: the Russian Revolution, which led the United States to send soldiers to northern Russia and Siberia

practice.explanation: In 1918 the United States was training millions of men for the war in Europe. Influenza spread through crowded camps and on the ships that carried soldiers overseas. Camp Funston had one of the first large outbreaks recorded in the United States, in March 1918.

whyNot.A: Army doctors fought yellow fever in Panama between 1904 and 1914. This photograph shows a camp in Kansas during the 1918 flu epidemic.
whyNot.B: U.S. troops did go into Mexico in 1916, but they came home early in 1917. Camps like this one trained men for the war in Europe.
whyNot.D: About 13,000 U.S. soldiers did go to Russia in 1918. But camps like this one trained millions of men for the war in France.

practice.hint: Use the attribution. Where and when was the photo taken, and what was happening in the world that year?

practice.stem: Doctors facing the epidemic in 1918 differed most from doctors facing epidemics after 1950 in that the doctors of 1918

options.A: did not believe that diseases could pass from one sick person to another
options.B: had no flu vaccines and no antibiotics to treat the infections that often followed the flu
options.C: did not yet know that mosquitoes could carry diseases such as malaria
options.D: relied mainly on new sulfa drugs, which later turned out to make patients with influenza worse

practice.explanation: The influenza virus was not identified until 1933. Flu vaccines came in the 1940s, and penicillin came into wide use during the Second World War. In 1918, care mostly meant rest, food, fresh air, and nursing.

whyNot.A: Doctors had understood germs since the late 1800s. That is why some workers in the photograph wear masks.
whyNot.C: Scientists had shown by 1900 that mosquitoes carry malaria and yellow fever.
whyNot.D: Sulfa drugs were not developed until the 1930s.

practice.hint: Think about which medical tools were invented after 1918.

practice.stem: The photograph would be most useful to a historian studying

options.A: how many people died of influenza in different countries around the world in 1918 and 1919
options.B: how the U.S. Army tried to care for large numbers of sick men during the epidemic
options.C: which medicines doctors found most effective in curing influenza
options.D: how the disease traveled from army camps in Kansas to Europe

practice.explanation: A photograph shows what one place looked like at one moment. This one shows how crowded the emergency hospitals became and how patients were cared for. Death counts or the spread of the disease would need other sources, such as records and reports.

whyNot.A: One photograph of one hospital cannot show how many people died around the world.
whyNot.C: The photograph shows beds and workers, not the medicines used or whether they worked.
whyNot.D: A photograph of one room cannot show the path of a disease across an ocean.

practice.hint: What can one picture of one room really show?

practice.stem: The concerns expressed in the declaration are best understood in the context of

options.A: a disease that had been nearly wiped out by vaccines but came back when vaccination programs ended
options.B: a disease that struck mostly older people as life expectancy in Africa rose
options.C: a new disease of the 1980s, with wide gaps between countries in access to prevention and treatment
options.D: a disease spread mainly by spoiled food and dirty water in the fast-growing cities of poor countries

practice.explanation: Doctors first reported AIDS in 1981. HIV is the virus that can cause it. By 2000 more than 36 million people were living with HIV, most of them in Africa south of the Sahara. High drug prices and few clinics left many people there without treatment. This 2001 meeting was the first special session of the UN General Assembly about a health problem.

whyNot.A: There has never been a vaccine for HIV. AIDS was a new disease, not an old one that came back.
whyNot.B: AIDS killed mostly young adults, not old people. That is why it lowered life expectancy.
whyNot.D: HIV spreads through blood, through sex, and from mother to baby, not through food.

practice.hint: Find the name of the disease in the first paragraph. Then check which choice really describes that disease.

practice.stem: Which of the following developments in the 2000s most directly addressed the problem described in paragraph 25?

options.A: Cheaper copies of AIDS drugs, and new funds such as the Global Fund that paid for treatment
options.B: The worldwide campaign that wiped out smallpox through vaccination
options.C: Programs in which the IMF and World Bank required poor countries to cut government spending
options.D: The founding of the World Health Organization to lead the fight against disease

practice.explanation: In 2001 an Indian drug company offered AIDS drugs for about a dollar a day per patient, far below the price of brand-name drugs. The Global Fund (2002) and the U.S. PEPFAR program (2003) paid for treatment. By 2010 millions of people in Africa were taking the drugs.

whyNot.B: Smallpox was wiped out by 1980, before AIDS spread widely. There is still no vaccine for HIV.
whyNot.C: These programs, called structural adjustment, often led poor countries to spend less on health. That made the problem worse.
whyNot.D: The WHO was founded in 1948. It existed long before the AIDS crisis, so its founding was not a response to it.

practice.hint: Paragraph 25 names two problems: what drugs cost and how they reach patients. When was each choice, and did it deal with either problem?

practice.stem: The declaration's claim that HIV/AIDS was "reversing or impeding development in many countries" is best supported by which of the following?

options.A: Life expectancy in China and India rose steadily from 1970 to 2020.
options.B: Deaths of children from measles fell sharply as vaccines spread after the 1980s.
options.C: Many East Asian economies grew quickly in the 1990s by making goods for export.
options.D: Life expectancy in several southern African countries fell by years between 1990 and 2005.

practice.explanation: In Botswana, Zimbabwe, South Africa, and other countries, AIDS killed many young adults. Life expectancy fell, families lost workers and parents, and millions of children became orphans. Years of progress were undone.

whyNot.A: This shows progress, not a reversal. China and India were not hit as hard by AIDS.
whyNot.B: This shows health getting better. The claim is about AIDS undoing progress.
whyNot.C: Fast growth in East Asia shows development going forward. AIDS was not the main health problem there.

practice.hint: Which choice gives evidence about the places and kind of harm the declaration describes?

practice.stem: The concern expressed in the second paragraph is best understood in the context of

options.A: the discovery in the 1980s of a hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica
options.B: acid rain from factory smoke, which damaged forests and lakes in Europe
options.C: scientific research since the 1950s showing that carbon dioxide in the air was rising
options.D: the oil crises of the 1970s, which raised fuel prices around the world

practice.explanation: From 1958, scientists measured carbon dioxide on a mountain in Hawaii and found it rising every year. In 1988 the UN helped set up a panel of scientists to study climate change. Its 1990 report helped lead to this treaty.

whyNot.A: The ozone hole was caused by chemicals called CFCs, used in spray cans and refrigerators. The convention is about gases that trap heat.
whyNot.B: Acid rain was a real problem, but it came from sulfur pollution. The convention is about warming of the Earth's surface.
whyNot.D: The oil crises raised prices. They were about the supply and cost of oil, not about warming.

practice.hint: The second paragraph says human activities are raising certain gases. How would anyone have known that?

practice.stem: The convention led most directly to which of the following?

options.A: The Kyoto Protocol, which set targets for richer countries to cut greenhouse gases
options.B: The Montreal Protocol, which phased out chemicals that harm the ozone layer
options.C: The founding of Greenpeace, which used direct protests to defend the environment
options.D: The Green Belt Movement in Kenya, which planted millions of trees

practice.explanation: In 1997 the countries that had joined the convention met in Kyoto, Japan. The Kyoto Protocol set targets for developed countries to cut their emissions. It set no targets for developing countries such as China and India, following the idea of "common but differentiated responsibilities."

whyNot.B: The Montreal Protocol was signed in 1987, five years before this convention.
whyNot.C: Greenpeace was founded in 1971, long before this convention.
whyNot.D: Wangari Maathai started the Green Belt Movement in 1977. It was a local movement, not a result of this treaty.

practice.hint: For each choice, ask whether it could have been shaped by a treaty signed in 1992.

practice.stem: Which of the following later developments would most directly challenge the way the convention divides the world into "developed" and "developing" countries?

options.A: Emissions per person stayed far higher in the United States than in India.
options.B: By 2006 China, still counted as a developing country, emitted more CO2 than the United States.
options.C: Millions of people in many developing countries still lived without electricity in their homes in 2020.
options.D: Rich countries pledged billions of dollars to help poor countries cope with floods, droughts, and rising seas.

practice.explanation: The convention put China and India with the developing countries, which had no targets under the Kyoto Protocol. But China's economy grew so fast that by 2006 it was the largest emitter in the world. Critics in the United States argued that a treaty without limits for China could not work. The 2015 Paris Agreement asked every country to set its own targets.

whyNot.A: This supports the convention. It says that emissions per person in developing countries are "still relatively low."
whyNot.C: This supports Article 4, which says that ending poverty is the first priority of developing countries.
whyNot.D: This follows the convention, which asks developed countries to provide "financial resources."

practice.hint: The convention treats two groups of countries differently. Which choice blurs the line between them?

practice.stem: The change in China's emissions from 1990 to 2024 is best explained by

options.A: heavy industry that Mao's government had built in the 1950s and 1960s
options.B: the growth of China's population to more than twice its 1990 size
options.C: the spread of chemical fertilizers to Chinese farms during the Green Revolution
options.D: factories making goods for world markets after China's economic reforms

practice.explanation: After Deng Xiaoping's reforms, and especially after China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, factories making goods for the world moved to China. Most of their energy came from burning coal. By 2006 China had passed the United States as the largest emitter.

whyNot.A: Mao's factories were built long before 1990. They cannot explain why emissions grew about five times after 1990.
whyNot.B: China's population grew from about 1.1 billion to about 1.4 billion. Its emissions grew about five times.
whyNot.C: Making fertilizer uses energy, but farming was a small part of China's emissions. Most came from coal burned in factories and power plants.

practice.hint: Compare China's bars for 1990 and 2024. Which choice could make emissions grow that much?

practice.stem: The drop in Russia's emissions between 1990 and 2010 most likely resulted from

options.A: Russia's Kyoto Protocol promise to cut its emissions far below its 1990 level
options.B: Russia's switch from coal to nuclear power after the Chernobyl accident
options.C: the collapse of much of Soviet industry after the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991
options.D: a fall in Russia's population to about half of what it had been in Soviet times

practice.explanation: When the Soviet Union broke up, many factories closed or made much less. Russia's economy shrank by about 40 percent in the 1990s. Emissions fell because of this collapse, not because of new environmental rules.

whyNot.A: Under the Kyoto Protocol, Russia only had to stay at or below its 1990 level. Its emissions had already fallen far below that before it joined in 2004.
whyNot.B: Few new nuclear plants were built after Chernobyl in 1986. Russia still burns large amounts of coal, oil, and gas.
whyNot.D: Russia's population fell only a little, from about 149 million to about 144 million.

practice.hint: Find the years when Russia's bar drops. What big political change happened in between?

practice.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the chart for comparing CO2 emissions per person in the places shown?

options.A: It does not show which fuels, such as coal, oil, or natural gas, each country burned.
options.B: It begins in 1970, so it leaves out the early years of industrialization.
options.C: It shows each country's total, though the countries' populations differ greatly.
options.D: It does not show other greenhouse gases, such as methane from farms and gas wells.

practice.explanation: China and India each have more than a billion people, so their totals are large even when emissions per person are lower. In 2024, U.S. emissions were about 14 tonnes per person and India's about 2. To find emissions per person, divide each total by the population. This average counts factories, power plants, and transport, not just what each person does.

whyNot.A: The kind of fuel helps explain the totals. But to compare one person with another, you need to know how many people live in each country.
whyNot.B: Earlier years matter for history. They do not help you compare people in the years the chart shows.
whyNot.D: The question asks only about CO2, so leaving out other gases does not get in the way.

practice.hint: Think about what you would need to know to compare emissions per person, not per country.

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Source 1 praises the world's existing economic order, while Source 2 calls for a new one.
options.B: Source 1 calls for more state control of the economy, while Source 2 calls for less.
options.C: Source 1 speaks mainly for the industrial countries, while Source 2 speaks for the developing countries.
options.D: Source 1 blames poverty on corrupt governments in developing countries, while Source 2 blames the industrial countries.

practice.explanation: In the 1970s many newly independent countries, working through the UN, asked for a "New International Economic Order." They wanted the right to take over foreign companies and to get better prices for their raw materials. By 1981 Reagan and other leaders, such as Margaret Thatcher in Britain, argued instead that free markets and trade were the path to growth.

whyNot.A: Source 1 says it is "impossible" to achieve balanced development "under the existing international economic order." It wants a new order.
whyNot.C: This reverses the sources. Source 1 speaks for the developing countries, which it says have "70 per cent of the world's population." Reagan was president of the United States.
whyNot.D: Source 1 blames the "existing international economic order," not corrupt governments. Reagan rejects the claim that the "capitalist United States is the cause of world hunger and poverty."

practice.hint: Sum up each source in one sentence. Then compare your two sentences with each choice.

practice.stem: The demands in Source 1 are best understood in the context of

options.A: the founding of the World Trade Organization, which set new rules for trade among its members
options.B: the debt crisis of the 1980s, when many developing countries could not repay foreign loans
options.C: the Marshall Plan, through which the United States gave aid to rebuild Western Europe
options.D: decolonization, which created many new states that together held a majority in the UN

practice.explanation: Between 1945 and 1975, dozens of colonies in Asia and Africa became independent. Each new country got a vote in the UN General Assembly. Together, the developing countries used their votes to pass this declaration in 1974, a few months after the Arab oil embargo showed how much power raw-material exporters could have.

whyNot.A: The WTO was founded in 1995, more than 20 years after this declaration.
whyNot.B: The debt crisis began in 1982, after this declaration. It later weakened the bargaining power of developing countries.
whyNot.C: The Marshall Plan rebuilt Western Europe after 1948. Source 1 is about the problems of developing countries.

practice.hint: Source 1 complains about a system set up long before 1974. What had changed in the world since then?

practice.stem: Ideas like those in Source 2 contributed most directly to which of the following in the 1980s and 1990s?

options.A: IMF loans that required countries to cut spending and open their markets
options.B: The founding of OPEC by oil-exporting countries to gain more control over oil prices
options.C: The takeover of foreign-owned oil and copper companies by governments in Latin America
options.D: The founding of the Non-Aligned Movement by leaders of newly independent countries

practice.explanation: In the 1980s many developing countries could not repay their debts. To get new loans from the IMF and the World Bank, they had to follow "structural adjustment" plans: cut government spending, sell state companies, and open their markets. Critics said these plans hurt the poor, and protests against the IMF and the World Bank spread.

whyNot.B: OPEC was founded in 1960. It gave governments more control over oil, which is closer to the ideas in Source 1.
whyNot.C: Taking over foreign companies matches Source 1's "right to nationalization," not Reagan's ideas. Most of these takeovers came in the 1960s and 1970s.
whyNot.D: The Non-Aligned Movement began in 1961. It was about staying out of the Cold War, not about free markets.

practice.hint: For each choice, ask: did it make the government's role in the economy bigger or smaller? Then compare with Reagan's view.

practice.stem: The "new policy" described in the second paragraph was a change from

options.A: the Nationalist government's land reforms and export factories on Taiwan in the 1960s
options.B: the Soviet Union's New Economic Policy, which allowed some private trade in the 1920s
options.C: Mao Zedong's policies of self-reliance and tight state control over the economy
options.D: the Qing dynasty's Self-Strengthening Movement, which borrowed Western military technology in the late 1800s

practice.explanation: Under Mao, China tried to develop on its own. Most industry was owned by the state, and most farming was done by large collectives. After Mao died in 1976, Deng Xiaoping began a policy of "reform and opening" in 1978. China welcomed foreign trade, investment, and technology.

whyNot.A: Those reforms happened on Taiwan, not in the People's Republic. Blumenthal is describing a change made by the leaders in Beijing.
whyNot.B: That was a Soviet policy of the 1920s. Blumenthal is describing a change in China's own policies.
whyNot.D: The Self-Strengthening Movement was a Qing policy of the 1800s. Blumenthal means the communist "policies and ideology of the past."

practice.hint: Blumenthal says the new policy is "contrary to the policies and ideology of the past." Whose past policies does he mean?

practice.stem: Blumenthal's purpose in writing the memorandum was most likely to

options.A: urge the president to cut off contact with China because its leaders could not be trusted
options.B: report to the president on the treatment of political prisoners he saw in China
options.C: persuade the president to sell American weapons to China for use against the Soviet Union
options.D: advise the president on how to handle economic relations with China

practice.explanation: Officials often write to the president after trips abroad. Blumenthal shares his impressions so that Carter can decide how far to go in building trade with China. He also warns that China's new course might not last.

whyNot.A: Blumenthal says China's leaders are determined to modernize and want "close trade and economic relations" with the United States. He sees an opportunity, not a reason to cut off contact.
whyNot.B: The memo is about China's economy and trade. It says nothing about prisoners.
whyNot.C: The memo is about trade and economic relations, not weapons sales.

practice.hint: Look at what the memo spends most of its time discussing.

practice.stem: Which of the following does Blumenthal use as evidence of the "inherent weaknesses" of China's economy?

options.A: A bicycle factory with a poor layout that relied on huge numbers of workers
options.B: The determination of Deng Xiaoping's government to modernize at a rapid pace
options.C: China's interest in close trade and economic relations with the United States
options.D: The huge size and hard work of China's labor force

practice.explanation: Blumenthal uses a visit to one factory as evidence. The factory made 1.7 million bicycles a year, but only by using 3,900 workers and old methods. He thought China would need foreign know-how to modernize. In 1980 China opened Special Economic Zones, where foreign companies could build modern factories.

whyNot.B: Blumenthal sees the leaders' drive to modernize as a reason for hope, not as a weakness.
whyNot.C: Close trade with the United States is what China's leaders want. Blumenthal does not call it a weakness.
whyNot.D: Blumenthal calls China's huge, hard-working labor force one of its "strengths."

practice.hint: Evidence is a specific fact or example. Find where Blumenthal discusses weaknesses, then check which choice he uses there.

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a pattern in the table?

options.A: The percentage of women in the labor force fell in most of the countries shown after 1990.
options.B: The largest increases came in East Asian countries with fast-growing economies, such as China and Japan.
options.C: The countries with the lowest rates in 1990 had the highest rates by 2024.
options.D: The percentage rose in most countries shown, but the levels still varied widely.

practice.explanation: After 1990 more women in many countries joined the labor force, helped by more schooling and new kinds of work. But culture, laws, and the kinds of jobs available kept the rates very different from place to place.

whyNot.A: It rose in seven of the nine countries listed. It fell in China and Egypt.
whyNot.B: China's rate fell from 73.1 to 59.4. Saudi Arabia and Bangladesh gained the most.
whyNot.C: Saudi Arabia rose a lot, but at 33.3 it was still far below Brazil or the United States.

practice.hint: Count how many countries went up and how many went down.

practice.stem: The change for Saudi Arabia shown in the table is best explained by

options.A: new oil discoveries in the 2010s that doubled Saudi Arabia's oil exports
options.B: a religious revival that urged Saudi women to leave paid work and stay at home
options.C: the arrival of garment factories making clothes for export, as in Bangladesh
options.D: reforms in the 2010s that opened more jobs to women and ended the ban on women driving

practice.explanation: Saudi Arabia had strict limits on women's work and travel. In 2017 the government announced that women could drive starting in 2018, and it opened many more jobs to women. The percentage of Saudi women in the labor force rose sharply after that.

whyNot.A: Saudi oil exports did not double. More oil money would also not explain why more women took jobs.
whyNot.B: This would have lowered the figure. The table shows that it more than doubled.
whyNot.C: Saudi Arabia's economy depends on oil, not on garment factories. Bangladesh's rise came partly from such factories.

practice.hint: Check each choice against what you know about Saudi Arabia's government and economy.

practice.stem: The data in the table would most directly challenge which of the following claims?

options.A: China's rapid economic growth after 1990 raised the percentage of Chinese women in the labor force.
options.B: In both years, women in South Asia were in the labor force at lower rates than women in the Americas.
options.C: The percentage of women in the U.S. labor force changed little after 1990.
options.D: The percentage of women in the labor force rose in parts of the Middle East after 1990.

practice.explanation: China's economy grew faster than almost any other after 1990, yet the percentage of Chinese women in the labor force fell. More young women stayed in school longer, and many state jobs disappeared. So fast growth does not by itself raise the percentage of women in the labor force.

whyNot.B: India (32.4) and Bangladesh (38.7) are below Brazil, Mexico, and the United States. The table supports this claim.
whyNot.C: The U.S. figure went from 56.0 to 56.6, almost no change. The table supports this claim.
whyNot.D: Saudi Arabia's figure more than doubled. The table supports this claim, even though Egypt's fell.

practice.hint: For each claim, find the countries it is about. Does the table agree or disagree?

practice.stem: The protests in Selma that Johnson describes are best understood as part of which broader development?

options.A: A labor movement in which factory workers in Northern cities went on strike for higher wages and benefits
options.B: An antiwar movement that opposed sending American soldiers to fight in Vietnam
options.C: A civil rights movement that used nonviolent protest, inspired partly by Gandhi in India
options.D: A Black nationalist movement that called for a separate state for African Americans in the South

practice.explanation: Martin Luther King Jr. and other leaders studied Gandhi's methods of nonviolent resistance. In March 1965, state police beat marchers who tried to walk from Selma to Montgomery. Johnson gave this speech eight days later.

whyNot.A: The Selma marchers wanted the right to vote, not higher wages.
whyNot.B: Protests against the Vietnam War were just beginning in 1965, but the Selma marches were about voting rights.
whyNot.D: The Selma marchers wanted equal rights as Americans. Johnson says they protested "the denial of their rights as Americans."

practice.hint: Johnson says the marchers "peacefully protested the denial of their rights as Americans." Which movement had that goal and that method?

practice.stem: Johnson's speech contributed most directly to

options.A: the Nineteenth Amendment, which gave American women the right to vote
options.B: the Voting Rights Act, which suspended literacy tests in many Southern states
options.C: the Supreme Court's ruling in Brown v. Board of Education against segregated schools
options.D: the Civil Rights Act, which banned segregation in hotels, restaurants, theaters, and other public places

practice.explanation: Congress passed the Voting Rights Act in August 1965. It stopped literacy tests in states with a history of keeping Black citizens from voting, and federal officials went to Southern counties to register Black voters. Within a few years, the share of Black adults registered to vote in the South rose sharply.

whyNot.A: The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920, decades earlier.
whyNot.C: The Brown decision came in 1954, eleven years before this speech.
whyNot.D: The Civil Rights Act became law in 1964, the year before this speech.

practice.hint: Johnson is asking Congress to pass a bill. What was the bill about?

practice.stem: The movement Johnson describes is most similar to which other movement of the second half of the twentieth century?

options.A: The struggle against apartheid in South Africa, which demanded equal rights regardless of race
options.B: The Cultural Revolution in China, in which young Red Guards attacked teachers and party officials
options.C: The Iranian Revolution, which replaced the shah with a government led by religious leaders
options.D: The movement for Quebec's independence, which sought a separate French-speaking country

practice.explanation: Both the U.S. civil rights movement and the anti-apartheid movement fought laws that kept people from voting because of their race. Both used protests, boycotts, and international attention. In 1994 all adult South African citizens, regardless of race, could vote in a national election.

whyNot.B: Mao launched the Cultural Revolution to attack his rivals. It was not a movement for equal voting rights.
whyNot.C: The Iranian Revolution set up a religious government. It was not a struggle for equal rights across races.
whyNot.D: Quebec separatists wanted to leave Canada. The Selma marchers wanted equal rights within the United States.

practice.hint: Compare the goals of each movement with the goal of the Selma marchers.

practice.stem: Based on Source 2, Mandela would most likely respond to the bill Harkin describes in Source 1 by arguing that

options.A: labor standards can be discussed, but rich countries should not ban imports on their own
options.B: child labor is a matter for each country alone and has no place in trade talks
options.C: the United States should ban the goods at once, since the Uruguay Round was fair to poor countries
options.D: poor countries should form their own trade bloc instead of joining the GATT's rules

practice.explanation: Many leaders of developing countries feared that rich countries would use labor rules as an excuse to block their exports. Mandela agreed that labor matters were important. But he insisted that rules be agreed on by all countries, not imposed by powerful ones such as the United States.

whyNot.B: Mandela says "there can be no refusal to discuss matters such as labour standards." He does not want the topic left out.
whyNot.C: Mandela says the Uruguay Round's rules did not fit the "realities" of developing countries. He also rejects bans that one country imposes on its own.
whyNot.D: Mandela wants to change the trading system from inside. He calls for listening and shared rules, not a separate bloc.

practice.hint: First decide what Harkin wants to do. Then find the parts of Source 2 that talk about that kind of action.

practice.stem: Concerns like those Mandela expresses in the second paragraph of Source 2 led most directly to

options.A: the creation of the euro as a shared currency for many European Union members
options.B: the Doha Round of WTO talks, which promised to focus on poor countries' needs
options.C: the signing of NAFTA, which lowered trade barriers among Canada, Mexico, and the United States
options.D: the Bretton Woods conference, which set up the IMF and the World Bank

practice.explanation: Developing countries argued that the Uruguay Round helped rich countries most. In 2001 the members of the World Trade Organization began new talks in Doha, Qatar, which they called a "development" round. The talks stalled for years, mostly over the payments rich countries made to their own farmers.

whyNot.A: The euro was a European plan to share one currency. It was not about how the GATT treated poor countries.
whyNot.C: NAFTA was signed in 1992, before this speech. It linked three countries in North America.
whyNot.D: The Bretton Woods conference was held in 1944, long before this speech.

practice.hint: Check the date of each choice. Then ask which one was meant to answer the complaints Mandela makes.

practice.stem: The debates reflected in both sources contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: The Arab Spring, in which protesters in North Africa demanded new governments
options.B: The anti-apartheid boycotts of South African goods in the 1980s
options.C: World Trade Organization rules that required members to protect workers' right to form unions
options.D: Large protests against the World Trade Organization's meeting in Seattle in 1999

practice.explanation: In 1999 tens of thousands of people protested at a WTO meeting in Seattle. They included labor unions worried about jobs and child labor, environmental groups, and activists from poor countries. The meeting ended without an agreement. Protests followed at later meetings of the WTO, the IMF, and the World Bank.

whyNot.A: The Arab Spring of 2010–2011 was a revolt against dictators. It was not about trade rules.
whyNot.B: Boycotts of South African goods came before these debates. They aimed to end apartheid, not to change trade rules.
whyNot.C: WTO members never agreed to rules requiring union rights. Many developing countries opposed such rules as a hidden way to block their exports.

practice.hint: Check each choice. Did it really happen, and was it a way for people who shared these worries to make themselves heard?

practice.stem: The phrase "barbarous acts which have outraged the conscience of mankind" refers most directly to

options.A: the Soviet blockade of West Berlin, which cut off food, coal, and other supplies to the city's people
options.B: the mass killings and other crimes of the Second World War, including the Holocaust
options.C: the civil war between China's Nationalists and Communists
options.D: the mass unemployment and hunger of the Great Depression

practice.explanation: The Universal Declaration was written just three years after the Second World War. The Nazis had murdered six million Jews and millions of others. The UN wanted to set standards so that such crimes would not happen again.

whyNot.A: The Berlin blockade was a Cold War standoff. The Western Allies flew in supplies, and it did not involve mass killing.
whyNot.C: The preamble mainly responds to the crimes of the Second World War, not to China's civil war, which was still being fought in 1948.
whyNot.D: The Depression caused great suffering, but it was an economic crisis, not "barbarous acts."

practice.hint: "Barbarous acts" means deliberate cruelty. Which events of the 1930s and 1940s most shocked the nations that wrote the Declaration?

practice.stem: Ideas like those in Article 2 contributed most directly to which of the following later developments?

options.A: The apartheid laws that separated South Africans by race in homes, schools, and jobs after 1948
options.B: Laws that gave voting and other rights to groups once shut out because of their race or sex
options.C: The growth of colonial armies to hold on to European colonies in Africa and Asia during the 1950s
options.D: Laws that guaranteed workers a minimum wage and paid vacations

practice.explanation: After 1948 many countries extended rights to people who had been left out. For example, women won the right to vote in Morocco in 1963 and in Swiss federal elections in 1971, and the U.S. Voting Rights Act of 1965 protected Black voters. Activists often pointed to the Declaration to support their causes.

whyNot.A: Apartheid made "distinction" by race the basis of the law, which Article 2 forbids.
whyNot.C: Colonial rule kept rights from the people who were ruled. Article 2 says everyone has the same rights, no matter what country or group they come from.
whyNot.D: Fair pay and paid vacations are rights named in other articles of the Declaration. Article 2 is about giving rights to everyone "without distinction of any kind."

practice.hint: Article 2 is about who gets rights. Which choice is about who gets rights, and does it follow Article 2 or go against it?

practice.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the Declaration as evidence of how people were actually treated around the world after 1948?

options.A: It does not say which countries voted for it and which did not.
options.B: It was adopted before most African colonies became independent nations.
options.C: It states rights people should have rather than showing whether governments protected them.
options.D: It uses broad words, such as "dignity," that people in different cultures might understand in different ways.

practice.explanation: The Declaration states a standard. It does not report how governments actually treated people, and many governments that voted for it still denied these rights at home. To learn how people were treated, historians need other sources, such as laws, court records, and eyewitness accounts.

whyNot.A: The vote matters if you are studying how the Declaration was adopted. It does not tell you how people were treated.
whyNot.B: This tells you who took part in writing it. It does not tell you how governments treated people later.
whyNot.D: Broad words can make the meaning harder to pin down. But even very clear words would not show whether governments obeyed them.

practice.hint: A limitation is a reason to be careful. Which choice could make the Declaration misleading as evidence of real life?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument of the white paper?

options.A: China plans to close its internet market to foreign companies in order to protect its own firms.
options.B: China welcomes the internet's growth but claims the right to control it within its borders.
options.C: China's citizens should be free to post whatever they wish as long as it is true.
options.D: The internet threatens China's economy and should be limited to government offices.

practice.explanation: The Chinese government wanted the economic benefits of the internet. But it also claimed "Internet sovereignty," the right to decide what could be posted inside China. Its system of filters and blocked foreign websites is often called the "Great Firewall."

whyNot.A: The paper says China will "open the Chinese Internet market in accordance with the law" and "welcome enterprises from other countries."
whyNot.C: The paper lists many kinds of information that no one may spread, such as anything "endangering state security." Truth is not the only test.
whyNot.D: The paper praises the internet's "irreplaceable role" in the economy and describes hundreds of millions of users.

practice.hint: Read the first and third paragraphs together. How does the paper balance them?

practice.stem: The policies described in the white paper are best understood in the context of

options.A: movements in Europe to protect local farmers from cheaper food imports
options.B: religious movements that rejected Western popular culture as a threat to traditional values
options.C: protests against IMF and World Bank programs that required cuts in government spending
options.D: state efforts to profit from global networks while limiting their political effects

practice.explanation: As the internet spread, China blocked many foreign websites, such as Facebook and Twitter. Chinese companies such as Baidu and Sina offered search and social media services while following state rules on content. Sina Weibo, a microblog launched in 2009, became hugely popular but had to remove posts the government banned. Other states, such as Iran, also built systems to control the internet.

whyNot.A: Farm protests were a response to trade in food. The white paper is about controlling information online.
whyNot.B: The white paper comes from a government, not a religious movement. Its limits are mostly about politics, such as "subverting state power."
whyNot.C: These protests were against economic rules set by global lenders. The paper is about a government controlling the internet.

practice.hint: Decide what the paper wants to gain from the internet and what it wants to avoid. Then find the broader pattern.

practice.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the white paper as evidence of how freely people in China could use the internet in 2010?

options.A: It gives figures for 2009 rather than for 2010.
options.B: It was written by the government that set and enforced the rules it describes.
options.C: It does not compare China's internet with that of other Asian countries.
options.D: It does not explain how the internet was first invented in the United States.

practice.explanation: A government report shows how that government wants its policies to be seen. It may not show how its rules worked in practice, such as which posts were deleted or who was punished. Historians would compare it with other sources, such as reports by journalists and human rights groups, and posts saved by users.

whyNot.A: Figures from 2009 are close enough to show how many people were online. The bigger question is whether the paper tells the whole story.
whyNot.C: A comparison would show how many people were online elsewhere. It would not show how freely people in China could use the internet.
whyNot.D: The internet's early history does not affect how freely people in China could use it in 2010.

practice.hint: A limitation is a reason to be careful. Which choice could make the paper misleading as evidence of how people actually used the internet?

practice.stem: Which of the following developments in the decade after the First World War most directly reflected the hopes Pankhurst expresses in the last paragraph?

options.A: Laws in Britain, the United States, and other countries that gave women the right to vote
options.B: The Treaty of Versailles, which made Germany pay reparations to the Allies
options.C: The return of many women to work in their homes after soldiers came back from the war
options.D: Treaties that limited the size of the navies of the great powers

practice.explanation: Women's war work strengthened the case for votes for women. Britain gave the vote to many women over 30 in 1918 and to all women on the same terms as men in 1928. Germany (1918), the United States (1920), and other countries also gave women the vote.

whyNot.B: The treaty set the terms of peace with Germany. It said nothing about women's right to vote.
whyNot.C: Many women did lose their wartime jobs when soldiers returned. That was the opposite of what Pankhurst hoped for.
whyNot.D: Naval treaties limited warships. Pankhurst's demand is "enfranchisement," the right to vote.

practice.hint: Reread the last paragraph. What exactly does Pankhurst want after the war ends?

practice.stem: Pankhurst's purpose in the last two paragraphs is most likely to

options.A: warn that the campaign for women's votes would start again after the war
options.B: announce that the women's movement had given up militant protest
options.C: urge women to refuse war work until they were given the vote
options.D: persuade British men to end the war by negotiating with Germany

practice.explanation: When the war began in August 1914, Pankhurst's group stopped its militant campaign and supported Britain's war effort. In this foreword she makes clear that the demand for the vote was only on hold. She also points to women's war work as proof that women deserved equal rights.

whyNot.B: Pankhurst says the struggle "has not been abandoned" but only "placed in abeyance," or paused.
whyNot.C: Pankhurst praises women for "keeping civilisation alive" with their war work. She does not ask them to stop.
whyNot.D: Pankhurst does not call for peace talks. She says the women's demand will return "when the clash of arms ceases."

practice.hint: Purpose means what the author wants readers to think or do. What does Pankhurst want readers to expect after the war?

practice.stem: Pankhurst's argument that women's war work should be rewarded is most similar to arguments made after the war by

options.A: anti-apartheid activists who called for sanctions against South Africa in the 1980s
options.B: environmental activists in the 1970s who warned that the Earth's resources could run out
options.C: free-market reformers who argued that lower taxes would speed economic growth
options.D: Indian nationalists who said India's service in the war had earned it self-rule

practice.explanation: About 1.3 million Indians served overseas in the First World War. Indian leaders expected self-government as a reward. When Britain offered only small reforms and passed harsh new laws in 1919, Gandhi led nationwide protests.

whyNot.A: Anti-apartheid activists wanted equal rights, but they did not claim that war service had earned them. Their method was outside pressure through sanctions.
whyNot.B: Environmental warnings were about protecting nature, not about rewards for service.
whyNot.C: Tax debates were about the economy, not about rights earned by service in war.

practice.hint: Focus on the kind of argument, not the topic. Pankhurst links service to a reward. Which choice uses the same kind of link?

practice.stem: The situation Cunliffe-Lister describes in the first paragraph is best understood in the context of

options.A: the spread of radio broadcasting, which let governments speak directly to millions of people
options.B: the rise of Bollywood films, which drew huge audiences across Asia and Africa
options.C: the rise of Hollywood studios, which dominated world film markets after the First World War
options.D: the growth of television, which drew audiences away from cinemas in Britain

practice.explanation: During the First World War, Europe's film studios shut down or shrank, while Hollywood grew. By the 1920s American films filled most of the world's cinema screens. Many governments worried that these films spread American tastes and products. Britain's law of 1927 required cinemas to show a rising share of British films.

whyNot.A: Radio did spread in the 1920s, but Cunliffe-Lister is talking about films shown in cinemas.
whyNot.B: Indian films did not fill the Empire's screens in 1927. Most films shown there came from the United States.
whyNot.D: Regular television broadcasts did not begin in Britain until 1936, and TV did not compete with cinemas until after the Second World War.

practice.hint: If only 5 percent of the films were British, where did most of the others come from?

practice.stem: The bill Cunliffe-Lister introduced is most similar to which later policy?

options.A: The Voice of America, a U.S. government radio service that broadcast news to other countries
options.B: The sale of worldwide television rights to the Olympic Games and the World Cup
options.C: Quotas in South Korea and France that required cinemas or TV channels to show a set share of films made at home
options.D: The spread of reggae music from Jamaica to audiences in Britain and around the world

practice.explanation: Many countries later used quotas to protect their films and TV from Hollywood. South Korea required cinemas to show Korean films on a set number of days each year, starting in the 1960s. France required TV channels to show mostly European works. Both countries argued that culture should not be treated like other trade goods.

whyNot.A: The Voice of America spread one country's views abroad. Cunliffe-Lister wanted to protect Britain's own films at home and in the Empire.
whyNot.B: Selling TV rights spread sports to world audiences. It did not protect national culture.
whyNot.D: The spread of reggae is an example of cultural globalization, not a policy to limit it.

practice.hint: First decide what kind of policy the bill is. Then look for a later policy of the same kind.

practice.stem: Cunliffe-Lister most likely mentions the report from New Zealand in order to

options.A: show that American films were changing what people in the Empire wanted to buy
options.B: argue that New Zealand should make more of the films shown in Britain and the Empire
options.C: prove that New Zealanders preferred British films to American ones
options.D: praise the people of New Zealand for keeping their "staunch British traditions"

practice.explanation: Cunliffe-Lister was speaking to the House of Commons, and he knew that many members cared about trade. By quoting an official in New Zealand, a loyal part of the Empire, he showed that American films were also selling American goods. This made his bill an economic issue as well as a cultural one.

whyNot.B: He wants more British-made films. He does not ask New Zealand to make films.
whyNot.C: The report says the opposite: tastes are moving away from "British habits and tastes."
whyNot.D: The report says that "even in New Zealand," with its British traditions, tastes were changing. It is a warning, not praise.

practice.hint: Look at the paragraph just before the quotation. What point is the quotation meant to prove?

practice.stem: The concerns about globalization in paragraph 5 are best understood in the context of

options.A: the Great Depression, when world trade collapsed and unemployment spread across the globe
options.B: financial crises in Asia, Russia, and Latin America in the late 1990s
options.C: the end of the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates in the early 1970s
options.D: the oil embargo of 1973–1974, which raised fuel prices around the world

practice.explanation: In 1997 investors suddenly pulled money out of Thailand, Indonesia, and South Korea. Their currencies crashed, and millions of people lost their jobs. Crises followed in Russia in 1998 and in Brazil in 1999. Many people asked whether global markets moved too fast for poorer countries to keep up.

whyNot.A: The Great Depression was a worldwide crisis, but it came 70 years earlier. The declaration is about globalization "at present."
whyNot.C: The Bretton Woods system ended in the early 1970s, long before this declaration.
whyNot.D: The oil embargo was a crisis of the 1970s. The declaration speaks of the challenge "we face today."

practice.hint: Which choice shows the costs of globalization falling on developing countries and "economies in transition"?

practice.stem: The goals in paragraph 19 led most directly to

options.A: eight Millennium Development Goals for 2015 that the UN tracked and later replaced with new goals for 2030
options.B: the founding of the World Bank to lend money to help rebuild countries after the Second World War
options.C: the Green Revolution, which used new seeds and fertilizer to raise grain harvests in Asia and Latin America
options.D: the creation of the WHO to fight diseases such as malaria and smallpox

practice.explanation: The goals in paragraph 19 became part of the eight Millennium Development Goals, which set targets for 2015. The UN tracked progress every year. By 2015 the share of people in extreme poverty had been cut by more than half, though many other targets were missed. In 2015 the UN adopted 17 Sustainable Development Goals for 2030.

whyNot.B: The World Bank was founded in 1944, long before this declaration.
whyNot.C: The Green Revolution began in the 1960s. It helped reduce hunger, but it came long before these goals.
whyNot.D: The WHO was founded in 1948. It worked on these diseases, but it was not created because of this declaration.

practice.hint: For each choice, ask whether it grew out of the promises in paragraph 19 or had other causes.

practice.stem: Which of the following would best support the declaration's claim that the benefits of globalization were "very unevenly shared"?

options.A: World trade grew faster than world output during the 1990s as many countries lowered their tariffs.
options.B: The number of people using the internet rose from a few million to hundreds of millions in the 1990s.
options.C: In the late 1990s the fifth of the world's people in the richest countries had 86 percent of world output.
options.D: Several East Asian countries, such as South Korea and Taiwan, grew rich by exporting goods to world markets.

practice.explanation: A 1999 UN report found that the fifth of the world's people in the richest countries had 86 percent of world output, while the poorest fifth had just 1 percent. Evidence about who gained, and how much, is what "unevenly shared" is about.

whyNot.A: Faster trade shows that globalization was growing. It does not show who got the benefits.
whyNot.B: This shows how fast the internet spread. It does not show whether its benefits were shared evenly.
whyNot.D: This shows that some countries gained from globalization. By itself it does not show that others were left behind.

practice.hint: Ask what kind of evidence would show that some people gained much more than others.

exam.title: Unit 9 Practice Exam: Globalization
exam.directions: Each set of questions refers to a source: a primary source, a historian's writing, an image, or data. For each question, choose the best answer. Use the source and your knowledge of world history from c. 1900 to the present. There is no penalty for guessing. Some sources use historical labels or words for groups of people that are no longer used; these words show the language of their time.

questions.stem: Gaud's contrast between the Green Revolution and a "Red Revolution like that of the Soviets" (second paragraph) is best understood in the context of

options.A: the rise of communist parties to power in most of Western Europe after the Second World War
options.B: the spread of import substitution policies, which used high tariffs to build up national industries in Latin America
options.C: the split between the Soviet Union and China, which divided the communist world in the 1960s and 1970s
options.D: competition between the United States and the Soviet Union for influence in newly independent nations

rationales.A: Incorrect. Communist parties were strong in France and Italy, but they did not take power in Western Europe. Gaud is talking about farming in Asia.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Import substitution was about building factories, not farming. Gaud's contrast is about which side poor nations would follow.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The split between the Soviet Union and China was real. But Gaud contrasts the Green Revolution with Soviet-style revolution in general. His point is about winning over poor nations.
rationales.D: Correct. In the 1960s the United States used food aid and farm help to win friends among new and poor nations. It hoped they would not turn to the Soviet model.

questions.explanation: During the Cold War, both superpowers tried to win over countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. American leaders hoped that more food would make poor countries less likely to have communist revolutions. Gaud chose the word "Green" to set his revolution apart from a "Red" one.

questions.stem: The developments Gaud describes contributed most directly to which of the following in the 1970s and 1980s?

options.A: A shift of most Asian farmland from food grains to export crops such as cotton, tea, jute, and rubber
options.B: Land reforms that broke up large estates and gave the land to poor farmers across India and Pakistan
options.C: Large gains in grain harvests in South and Southeast Asia that helped feed fast-growing populations
options.D: The replacement of rice by wheat as the main food crop in most of Southeast Asia

rationales.A: Incorrect. The new seeds were mostly food grains such as wheat and rice, and food harvests grew. Asian farmland did not switch mainly to export crops.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Green Revolution spread new seeds and fertilizer. It did not take land from big owners and give it to the poor.
rationales.C: Correct. The new seeds spread across Asia. India's grain harvests more than doubled between the mid-1960s and 1990, and large famines became rare there.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Rice stayed the main food in Southeast Asia. New kinds of rice, such as IR-8, made rice harvests bigger.

questions.explanation: With new seeds, fertilizer, and irrigation, countries such as India, Pakistan, Indonesia, and the Philippines grew much more grain. This helped feed billions more people. It also made farmers depend more on chemicals and on water for irrigation.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly qualify Gaud's argument that the Green Revolution was "beneficial to mankind"?

options.A: Larger farmers gained the most, since many small farmers could not afford the fertilizer and water the seeds needed.
options.B: Wheat harvests in India and Pakistan rose to record levels in the late 1960s, soon after farmers began planting the new seeds.
options.C: The Soviet Union's collective farms also raised their grain harvests in the late 1960s.
options.D: Governments in South Asia lent farmers money to buy seeds and fertilizer, and they built new irrigation canals and wells.

rationales.A: Correct. Gaud admits the new rice cost four times as much to grow. If poor farmers could not pay, the benefits were uneven. That limits, or qualifies, his claim.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Record harvests support Gaud's argument. They do not limit it.
rationales.C: Incorrect. This might weaken Gaud's contrast with a "Red Revolution," but it says nothing about whether the Green Revolution helped or hurt people.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Loans and irrigation are the kind of "sound agricultural policies" Gaud praises. This supports his argument.

questions.explanation: The Green Revolution did grow much more food. But in some places it widened the gap between rich and poor farmers. It also used large amounts of fertilizer, pesticides, and water. Evidence like this qualifies Gaud's very hopeful view.

questions.stem: The report's account of how influenza spread across India (first paragraph) best illustrates which broader development of the early twentieth century?

options.A: New vaccines sent by railway to rural villages helped slow the spread of disease in the colonies.
options.B: Networks of railways, ships, and mail that linked regions also carried disease quickly from place to place.
options.C: Indian nationalists used the railways and the post to organize boycotts of British goods during the epidemic.
options.D: Indentured workers leaving India for plantations abroad carried the disease mainly to the Caribbean.

rationales.A: Incorrect. There was no working flu vaccine in 1918. Scientists did not identify the flu virus until the 1930s.
rationales.B: Correct. The report says that trains full of people fleeing the cities, the post, and travelers spread the infection. The networks that moved people and goods around the world in 1918 also moved the flu.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Gandhi's first nationwide boycott campaign began in 1920, after the epidemic. The report says the trains and the post spread infection, not protest.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Britain stopped sending indentured workers from India abroad in 1917. The report is about the disease spreading inside India.

questions.explanation: In 1918 the flu traveled along the busiest routes in the world: railways, shipping lanes, and the routes of armies. The report shows how these networks carried infection from place to place in the provinces it covered.

questions.stem: The report's statement that "a similar need depleted the civil medical practitioners in all countries taking part in the late struggle" best supports which conclusion?

options.A: Doctors trained in India had been sent to Europe to fight the influenza epidemic there.
options.B: The First World War weakened the ability of many societies to care for the sick during the pandemic.
options.C: Colonial India suffered fewer deaths from the disease than the European countries that fought in the war.
options.D: Governments in the warring countries trained many new doctors during the war to meet the needs of civilians.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The report says doctors were supplied "for the war," not to fight influenza in Europe.
