rationales.B: Correct. Armies took doctors away from ordinary people just as the flu struck. The report says this happened "in all countries taking part" in the war, not only in India.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The report describes a huge death toll, about 7 million, and a shortage of doctors. It does not show that India suffered fewer deaths than other places.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The report says the war "depleted" civilian doctors. That means there were fewer of them, not more.

questions.explanation: The pandemic struck in the last months of the First World War. Doctors and nurses were serving with armies, and crowded camps and troopships helped the disease spread. India alone sent more than a million soldiers and workers overseas during the war.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the report as evidence for the number of people who died of influenza in 1918 in the areas it covers?

options.A: The passage does not say which medicines worked best against the disease.
options.B: The report was printed in English, which most people in India could not read.
options.C: The passage does not describe how people in India felt about the British government's response to the epidemic.
options.D: The author could only estimate flu deaths, since the records mixed them with deaths from other diseases.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Medicines are a different question. Leaving them out does not make the death count less reliable.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The language of the report affects who could read it, not whether its count of deaths is right.
rationales.C: Incorrect. People's feelings about the government are a different topic. They do not change how many people died.
rationales.D: Correct. The report says "there is no method" to count flu deaths exactly. It admits that deaths from plague, cholera, malaria, and other diseases were mixed into the records, so it gives an average of several estimates.

questions.explanation: Death records in India in 1918 were incomplete. Many deaths were never recorded, or were listed under "fever." So the report could only estimate. Later historians, using other methods and covering more of South Asia, have estimated much higher totals.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a pattern shown in the chart?

options.A: Life expectancy rose faster in Japan than in any other country shown in the years after 1970.
options.B: Life expectancy fell in most of the countries shown during the years between 1990 and 2005.
options.C: Life expectancy rose over the period in each country, but Japan and Nigeria stayed far apart.
options.D: By 2023, life expectancy in India had passed life expectancy in China.

rationales.A: Incorrect. China rose about 21 years (56.8 to 78.0). Japan rose about 12. China's gain was bigger.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Most countries kept rising from 1990 to 2005. Only South Africa and Botswana fell.
rationales.C: Correct. Each country's figure for 2023 is higher than for 1970. But life expectancy in Japan (84.0) was still about 30 years higher than in Nigeria (54.5).
rationales.D: Incorrect. India reached 72.0 in 2023. That is still below China's 78.0.

questions.explanation: After 1950, vaccines, antibiotics, clean water, and more food helped people live longer almost everywhere. But poorer countries with weak health systems, such as Nigeria, still lag far behind richer ones.

questions.stem: The change for South Africa and Botswana between 1990 and 2005 was most likely caused by

options.A: an Ebola epidemic that spread from West Africa to the southern part of the continent
options.B: the return of a deadly influenza like that of 1918 to Africa's crowded cities
options.C: the spread of HIV, which infected a large share of adults in southern Africa
options.D: a famine that followed the collapse of farming in South Africa's apartheid-era homelands

rationales.A: Incorrect. The largest Ebola outbreak hit West Africa in 2014–2016, after 2005. It did not reach southern Africa.
rationales.B: Incorrect. No influenza outbreak like that of 1918 hit Africa in these years.
rationales.C: Correct. By the early 2000s about one in four adults in Botswana had HIV. Before treatment was available, AIDS killed many young adults, which pulled life expectancy down.
rationales.D: Incorrect. South Africa did not have a famine in these years. Also, life expectancy fell in Botswana too (from 60.1 to 54.4), and Botswana never had apartheid.

questions.explanation: HIV is the virus that can lead to AIDS. Before good treatment was widely available, AIDS caused many early deaths, and southern Africa was hit especially hard. Medicines that stop HIV from multiplying, paid for in part by the Global Fund and the U.S. PEPFAR plan, helped life expectancy rise again after 2005.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains both the overall gains and the setbacks shown in the chart?

options.A: Economic growth in the countries that were already wealthy in 1970 raised life spans mainly in those countries.
options.B: Falling fertility rates in poorer countries raised life spans there and caused the drops in southern Africa.
options.C: The end of colonial rule in Africa raised life spans there faster than in the countries of Asia.
options.D: Wider access to medicine, clean water, and food raised life spans, but major epidemics could reverse gains.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Some of the biggest gains came in China and India, which were poor in 1970.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Lower fertility alone does not explain longer lives, and it cannot explain the sharp drops in South Africa and Botswana between 1990 and 2005.
rationales.C: Incorrect. India gained about 23 years and China about 21. Nigeria gained about 15, less than either.
rationales.D: Correct. Most countries rose steadily, and India gained more than 23 years. But South Africa and Botswana fell between 1990 and 2005 before rising again.

questions.explanation: Vaccines, antibiotics, and better food and water spread across the world after 1950, and the Green Revolution helped feed growing populations. But HIV showed that a new epidemic could still undo years of progress.

questions.stem: The photograph was made possible most directly by

options.A: a joint space program that the United States and the Soviet Union ran together through the United Nations
options.B: government spending on rockets during the Space Race between the two superpowers
options.C: the invention of color film, which first became available to photographers in the 1960s
options.D: communication satellites that carried live television pictures between continents

rationales.A: Incorrect. The two superpowers competed in space in the 1960s. Their first joint mission came in 1975.
rationales.B: Correct. The Space Race grew out of the Cold War. After the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957, the United States poured money into NASA and the Apollo program.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Color film had been sold since the 1930s. Apollo 8 could reach the Moon only because the government spent billions on the space program.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Satellites did carry live television, and Apollo 8 sent TV pictures home. But this photograph was taken on film and developed after the astronauts returned to Earth.

questions.explanation: Apollo 8 was the first spacecraft with a crew to orbit the Moon. It was part of the Space Race, which pushed fast advances in rockets, computers, and communication.

questions.stem: Images such as this one contributed most directly to which of the following in the 1970s?

options.A: The Outer Space Treaty, which banned nuclear weapons in orbit and on the Moon
options.B: Arms control agreements, such as SALT I, that limited the number of nuclear missiles
options.C: The growth of environmental movements that urged people to protect the Earth as a shared home
options.D: The oil crises of 1973 and 1979, which raised fuel prices around the world

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Outer Space Treaty was signed in 1967, before this photograph was taken.
rationales.B: Incorrect. SALT I came out of talks between the superpowers about their weapons, not out of pictures of Earth.
rationales.C: Correct. Seeing the whole Earth, small and alone in space, helped people think of it as fragile. The first Earth Day was held in 1970, and groups such as Greenpeace began soon after.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The oil crises were caused by war and revolution in the Middle East, not by photographs.

questions.explanation: Photographs like this one were printed in magazines and shown on television around the world. They became symbols for the environmental movement, which grew quickly in the 1970s.

questions.stem: The photograph's rapid spread around the world in the late 1960s is best understood as part of which broader development?

options.A: The worldwide spread of consumer brands such as Coca-Cola and Toyota
options.B: The growth of tourism as jet airliners let more people travel to other countries
options.C: The growth of mass media, such as television and magazines, that let people everywhere share events
options.D: The spread of rock and roll and other American popular music to Europe and Asia

rationales.A: Incorrect. Global brands spread in these years too, but brands did not make this photograph famous. Television, magazines, and newspapers did.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Jet travel did grow in the 1960s, but mass media, not travelers, carried this photograph to huge audiences.
rationales.C: Correct. Television and magazines carried space images to huge audiences. Many millions of people around the world watched Apollo 8's broadcast from orbit around the Moon on Christmas Eve 1968.
rationales.D: Incorrect. American music did spread around the world, but it has nothing to do with how people saw this photograph.

questions.explanation: After the Second World War, television spread around the world. By the mid-1960s, satellites could send live TV from one continent to another. Events such as the Moon missions and the Olympic Games became things people everywhere watched together.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two speeches?

options.A: De Klerk asks other nations to keep their sanctions on South Africa, while Mandela asks them to lift sanctions.
options.B: De Klerk says talks should begin now, while Mandela says further steps must come first.
options.C: De Klerk rejects voting rights for Black South Africans, while Mandela calls for universal suffrage.
options.D: De Klerk speaks mainly to foreign governments, while Mandela speaks mainly to white South African voters.

rationales.A: Incorrect. This reverses the speakers. Mandela is the one who asks the world "to continue the campaign to isolate the apartheid regime."
rationales.B: Correct. De Klerk says "the time for talking has arrived." Mandela praises him. But Mandela says two things must happen before real talks can start: the state of emergency must end, and all political prisoners must go free.
rationales.C: Incorrect. De Klerk lists "universal franchise" among his aims, so he does not reject voting rights for Black South Africans. The two leaders still disagreed about other details.
rationales.D: Incorrect. De Klerk spoke to Parliament, and Mandela spoke to a crowd of supporters. Mandela speaks of "our people" and "our own decisive mass action."

questions.explanation: In February 1990 both leaders said they wanted to end apartheid through talks. But they disagreed about the pace. De Klerk wanted talks to start at once, while Mandela and the ANC wanted pressure kept on the government until more of their demands were met.

questions.stem: De Klerk's claim that 1989 was "the year in which Stalinist communism expired" (Source 1) refers most directly to

options.A: the victory of communist parties in elections in several countries of southern Africa
options.B: China's decision to hold free elections for a new government after the protests in Tiananmen Square
options.C: the withdrawal of the Soviet army from Afghanistan after ten years of fighting there
options.D: the fall of communist governments in Poland, East Germany, and other Eastern European countries

rationales.A: Incorrect. Communist parties did not win power in southern Africa in 1989. De Klerk is saying that communism had failed.
rationales.B: Incorrect. China's government crushed the Tiananmen protests in June 1989 and kept one-party rule.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Soviet army did leave Afghanistan early in 1989, but the communist government there held power until 1992. De Klerk points to the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe.
rationales.D: Correct. In 1989 communist rule began to collapse across Eastern Europe, and the Berlin Wall was opened in November. De Klerk says this collapse "served as a warning" to communists in Africa.

questions.explanation: The fall of communist governments in Eastern Europe weakened the South African government's argument that ending apartheid would bring a Soviet-backed takeover. This made it easier for de Klerk to lift the bans. He also hoped to end the sanctions that were hurting South Africa's economy.

questions.stem: Mandela's call for the international community "to continue the campaign to isolate the apartheid regime" (Source 2) refers most directly to

options.A: economic sanctions and boycotts by many governments and groups
options.B: the Cold War policy of containment, which aimed to stop the spread of Soviet influence in Africa
options.C: the armed struggle carried out by the ANC's military wing inside South Africa
options.D: the Non-Aligned Movement's refusal to take sides in the Cold War

rationales.A: Correct. Many countries limited trade with and investment in South Africa in the 1980s, and the UN banned the sale of weapons to it. Sports teams and musicians also boycotted the country.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Containment was a U.S. policy aimed at the Soviet Union. Some Western leaders even treated South Africa's government as an anti-communist ally.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The armed struggle was the ANC's own action inside South Africa. Mandela is asking the "international community" to act.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Staying out of the Cold War is a different issue. Mandela is talking about cutting South Africa off from the world.

questions.explanation: International pressure on South Africa grew in the 1980s. Sanctions (limits on trade and other ties, used to pressure a government) cut foreign investment and hurt its economy. Mandela feared that lifting them too early would take away the pressure on the government.

questions.stem: The developments described in the two speeches led most directly to

options.A: the creation of separate "homelands" in which Black South Africans were required to live and hold citizenship
options.B: a civil war that split South Africa into a white-ruled state and a Black-ruled state
options.C: South Africa's first national election in which all adult citizens could vote, held in 1994
options.D: the return of the ban on the ANC after the National Party won the next election held for white voters

rationales.A: Incorrect. The homelands were set up under apartheid, years before 1990. The talks of the 1990s ended them.
rationales.B: Incorrect. There was violence during the years of talks, but no civil war split the country. South Africa stayed one country.
rationales.C: Correct. After four years of talks, South Africa held its first national election open to all adult citizens, regardless of race, in April 1994. The ANC won, and Mandela became president.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The ban on the ANC was never brought back. In 1992 white voters approved continuing the talks in a referendum.

questions.explanation: De Klerk's reforms and Mandela's release began years of hard bargaining. In 1993 Mandela and de Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize. In 1994 Mandela became South Africa's first Black president.

questions.stem: The agreement is best understood as part of which broader trend of the late twentieth century?

options.A: A move by many governments toward free-market policies that lowered barriers to trade and investment
options.B: Calls by developing countries for a New International Economic Order that would raise the prices of raw materials
options.C: The use of import substitution, in which high tariffs protected new national industries from foreign goods
options.D: The growth of state-run industries, such as the oil companies taken over by Mexico and Venezuela

rationales.A: Correct. NAFTA aimed to "eliminate barriers to trade" and "increase substantially investment opportunities." In the 1980s and 1990s many countries, including Mexico, cut tariffs, sold state companies, and welcomed foreign investment.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The New International Economic Order of the 1970s asked for more state control over trade and foreign companies. NAFTA did the opposite: it opened markets.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Import substitution used high tariffs to keep foreign goods out. NAFTA's goal was to remove such barriers.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Government takeovers of industries were common from the 1930s to the 1970s. NAFTA protects investors and "intellectual property rights," which points the other way.

questions.explanation: After the debt crisis of the 1980s, many governments moved away from state control of the economy. Mexico sold hundreds of state companies and joined the GATT in 1986. NAFTA, which took effect in 1994, removed most tariffs among Canada, Mexico, and the United States.

questions.stem: The authors of the agreement most likely included Article 104 in order to

options.A: let Mexico keep foreign companies out of its national oil industry
options.B: show that the free trade area followed the rules of the GATT, the main treaty on world trade
options.C: make sure that state and provincial governments would obey the agreement
options.D: answer critics who feared that freer trade would weaken protections for the environment

rationales.A: Incorrect. Mexico did keep its oil industry under state control, but other parts of the agreement dealt with that. Article 104 is about environmental treaties.
rationales.B: Incorrect. That is the purpose of Article 101, which names the GATT. Article 104 names environmental treaties.
rationales.C: Incorrect. That is the purpose of Article 105. Article 104 is about what happens when NAFTA conflicts with environmental treaties.
rationales.D: Correct. Article 104 says that if NAFTA conflicts with three environmental treaties, those treaties "shall prevail." During the debate, environmental groups warned that trade rules could override laws protecting wildlife, the ozone layer, and the safe disposal of waste.

questions.explanation: Many environmental and labor groups opposed NAFTA. They feared that factories would move to places with weaker rules. To win support, the three governments also signed side agreements on the environment and on labor in 1993.

questions.stem: Which of the following was a response to the agreement when it took effect?

options.A: An armed uprising by the Zapatistas, a mostly Indigenous group in the Mexican state of Chiapas
options.B: The founding of Mercosur, a trade bloc of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay
options.C: The Mexican government's takeover of the country's private banks during a debt crisis
options.D: The signing of the Maastricht Treaty, which created the European Union

rationales.A: Correct. The Zapatistas rose up on January 1, 1994, the day NAFTA took effect. They said that free trade, along with a 1992 change in Mexico's land laws, would ruin poor Indigenous farmers.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Mercosur was founded in 1991, before NAFTA was signed. It was a South American trade bloc, not a response to NAFTA.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Mexico's government took over the banks in 1982, during the debt crisis. It sold them again in the early 1990s.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1992, before NAFTA took effect. It was a European plan, not a response to NAFTA.

questions.explanation: The Zapatistas took their name from Emiliano Zapata, a hero of the Mexican Revolution. Their revolt was one of the first well-known protests against global trade. Their supporters used fax machines and the early internet to spread their message around the world.

questions.stem: The government actions described in the third and fourth paragraphs are best understood as part of which broader pattern?

options.A: Efforts by some states to limit the political and cultural effects of global communication networks
options.B: Attempts by governments to keep out foreign films and music to protect their own entertainment industries
options.C: Laws passed in many countries to protect internet users' privacy from large technology companies
options.D: Programs run through the United Nations to share internet equipment with poorer countries

rationales.A: Correct. Clinton describes governments that censor the internet, block social networking sites, and erase words from searches. These states wanted the benefits of the internet without its political risks.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Some countries did limit foreign films and music, but Clinton is describing the blocking of news, ideas, and online networks.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The governments Clinton describes were watching and limiting what people saw online, not protecting them.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Clinton describes barriers between people and the world's networks, not the sharing of equipment.

questions.explanation: As the internet spread after 2000, some governments built filters and blocked foreign websites. China's system, often called the "Great Firewall," is the best-known example. At the same time, Chinese companies such as Sina Weibo and Baidu grew up under government rules.

questions.stem: Clinton's phrase "a new information curtain is descending" compares internet censorship with

options.A: the rules for European colonial claims in Africa set at the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885
options.B: the division of Europe between communist and noncommunist states after World War II
options.C: the partition of British India into the separate countries of India and Pakistan in 1947
options.D: the long walls that the Ming dynasty built along China's northern frontier against invaders

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Berlin Conference set rules for claiming colonies in Africa. It was not about blocking the flow of information.
rationales.B: Correct. In 1946 Winston Churchill said that an "iron curtain" had descended across Europe, cutting the communist East off from the West. Clinton echoes his words.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The partition of India divided land and people by religion. Clinton's "curtain" is about blocking information, like the Cold War barrier.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Ming walls were built to keep out invaders from the north. Clinton's words echo a phrase from the twentieth century.

questions.explanation: Clinton suggests that the struggle over the free flow of information is like the Cold War. During the Cold War, communist governments jammed Western radio and banned many books and newspapers. Some governments today try to block parts of the internet.

questions.stem: Clinton's comparison of "connection technologies" with the Green Revolution (last paragraph) suggests that she sees these technologies mainly as

options.A: tools that could help poor countries grow richer by spreading knowledge and access to markets
options.B: threats to farmers in poor countries who depend on traditional seeds and ways of making a living
options.C: services that poor countries would not be able to afford for many more decades
options.D: replacements for foreign aid, which she says governments should stop giving

rationales.A: Correct. The Green Revolution is often praised for growing far more food. Clinton hopes the internet and mobile phones will do something similar for economic growth in poor countries.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Clinton presents these technologies as a help to poor people, not a threat.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Clinton says these technologies "can do for economic growth what the Green Revolution did for agriculture." She expects them to help poor countries soon, not decades later.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Clinton does not say that aid should stop. She compares the internet to the Green Revolution, which foreign aid helped pay for.

questions.explanation: By 2010, mobile phones were spreading fast in Africa and South Asia. Farmers could check prices and send money by phone. Clinton hoped this would help poor countries join the global economy.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a pattern shown in the chart?

options.A: Internet use grew more slowly in China than in Nigeria between 2000 and 2022, so Nigeria caught up with China.
options.B: Internet use in the United States fell after 2010 as Americans switched from home computers to mobile phones.
options.C: Internet use grew faster in Nigeria than in India between 2010 and 2022.
options.D: From 2010 to 2022, India, Mexico, and China closed much of their internet-use gap with richer countries.

rationales.A: Incorrect. China rose from 1.8 to 75.6 percent. Nigeria rose from 0.1 to 39.1 percent.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The U.S. figure rose from 71.7 to 92.7 percent. Use on mobile phones counts as internet use.
rationales.C: Incorrect. India rose from 7.5 to 55.9 percent, a gain of about 48 points. Nigeria rose from 11.5 to 39.1, a gain of about 28.
rationales.D: Correct. From 2010 to 2022, India rose from 7.5 to 55.9 percent, Mexico from 31.1 to 78.6, and China from 34.3 to 75.6. The United States, South Korea, and Finland rose by much less, since they were already near the top.

questions.explanation: Cheap smartphones and mobile networks spread the internet quickly after 2010, and with it social media, online video, and shopping. Still, in 2022 about two in five Nigerians used the internet, compared with nearly all South Koreans.

questions.stem: The high rates of internet use in South Korea, Finland, and the United States by 2010 are best explained by

options.A: industrialization based mainly on making goods at home instead of importing them
options.B: the growth of knowledge economies built on information technology, research, and services
options.C: the spread of container shipping, which lowered the cost of trade between continents
options.D: the growth of factory economies in Asian countries such as Vietnam and Bangladesh

rationales.A: Incorrect. This strategy, called import substitution, was used mostly in Latin America and other developing regions in the mid-1900s. It does not explain high internet use in these countries.
rationales.B: Correct. These countries spent heavily on education, research, and computer networks. Companies such as Samsung in South Korea and Nokia in Finland made phones and network equipment.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the chart for a historian studying how freely people could share information online?

options.A: It counts internet users but does not show whether governments blocked what they could see.
options.B: It does not show how many people in each country owned a computer at home.
options.C: It leaves out the years before 2000, when the internet was first spreading.
options.D: It does not include any country in Europe except Finland.

rationales.A: Correct. A high number of users does not mean a free internet. Three in four Chinese people were online in 2022, but China's government blocks many foreign websites.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Owning a computer is about access. People can go online in other ways, and access does not show freedom.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Earlier years would help a study of how the internet began, not of how freely people could share information.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Adding more European countries would not show whether governments blocked what people could see.

questions.explanation: The chart counts how many people went online. It does not show whether they could read or say what they wanted. To study that, a historian would need other evidence, such as government rules and reports by journalists and human rights groups.
